messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Holt is a 46-year-old graphic designer of European descent who lives with his wife in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant deterioration in his functioning over the past eighteen months, presenting with a PCL-5 score of 65. The events that brought him to this point began on an otherwise unremarkable evening when Marcus was stopped by police officers while walking home from a late client meeting. What followed was not a brief procedural encounter. Officers restrained him against a wall, and during the altercation one officer struck him repeatedly. Marcus sustained visible lacerations to his face and a deep bruise across his ribs. He lay on the pavement for several minutes before anyone helped him. No charges were filed against the officers. No formal investigation was opened. He was simply left there, bleeding, and told to go home.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found that the memory of the incident did not behave like an ordinary memory. It did not sit in the past. Instead, something in his surroundings — the flash of a uniform, a police siren three blocks away, or even the sight of a stranger's bruised arm — could instantly collapse the distance between then and now, returning him to the pavement with a completeness that left him breathless. These triggers did not simply remind him of what happened; they detonated it. His body would flood with alarm, his chest tighten, and the sense of imminent danger would arrive fully formed, as though the attack were still ongoing. When a trigger struck, the full memory surged back with it, and the two fed each other — the alarm in his body confirming that the threat was real, the memory supplying the evidence.

What made this worse, in ways Marcus struggled to articulate even to himself, was the belief that had quietly taken root in him: that what was done to him was profoundly unjust, that nothing had been done about it, and that his life had been irreparably destroyed. He had come to feel that the world he once moved through with reasonable confidence was no longer his world. These convictions did not stay contained. Because he had come to believe that authority figures represented unaddressed danger, the sight of any police presence was not merely unpleasant — it was a confirmation that he remained unprotected, and his body responded accordingly, snapping back to high alert. The same beliefs coloured the memory itself: when the injustice felt most vivid, the memory felt most raw, and he would find himself revisiting the pavement again without choosing to.

When he tried to explain what had happened — to his wife, briefly, or to his GP — he would lose the thread entirely, the emotion rising so fast that he had to stop. He could not finish the account. The overwhelm was total. And so he stopped trying to explain, and started trying not to think. He began spending long hours on his phone, cycling through games and social media, keeping his mind occupied every waking moment so that nothing could surface. He withdrew from friends and, increasingly, from his wife. At his design studio, where he had once worked with easy concentration, he now sat behind his screen for different reasons — not creating, but escaping. Deadlines slipped. A long-standing client relationship ended. His wife had begun to ask questions he could not answer.

The avoidance, however, did not protect him. By keeping his mind perpetually busy, Marcus never fully processed what had happened, and the memory remained as volatile and fragmented as ever. When distraction occasionally failed — a notification sound that echoed a radio dispatch, a news image of a man with a bloodied face — the memory broke through with renewed force, and his body, already primed by weeks of unresolved tension, was instantly back on alert. He could not relax anywhere. Before entering any room, he noted the exits. His muscles had not fully unclenched in over a year.

Marcus sought help now because his wife told him quietly one evening that she was frightened — not of him, but for him. What he fears most is that nothing can be made right, that the injustice is permanent and the damage is done. What he is hoping for, though he can barely say it, is that he might one day feel safe in his own body again.
